title: Are You Focusing On The Wrong Students?
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin challenges the common assumption that one or two extremely difficult students are the true source of classroom disorder. He argues that a second, larger group of students—typically six to eight—who engage in smaller 'quality of life' misbehaviors like calling out, side-talking, and leaving their seats, actually provoke and enable the more visible misbehavior of the most challenging few. Linsin contends that difficult students don't need extra reminders, pep-talks, or behavior contracts; instead, teachers should focus their energy on shaping this larger middle group into positive role models. As more students buy into good behavior, the article claims, even the most difficult students eventually fall in line simply because the social environment no longer supports their misbehavior. The piece closes by framing this as a comprehensive, class-wide approach rather than a targeted intervention.
points: A widely held but flawed belief is that one or two difficult students are responsible for most classroom misbehavior.
A second group of six-to-eight students engaging in smaller everyday misbehaviors is identified as the real driver of classroom disorder, since they model and provoke bigger problems.
Difficult students need less individualized attention—not more—including fewer reminders, pep-talks, and behavior contracts.
The recommended strategy is to teach, model, and require exceptional behavior from all students from day one, building a class-wide culture of good conduct.
As the majority of the class buys into positive behavior, the pull of that culture eventually brings even the most challenging students into line.
quotes: A second group of students would emerge from the mist. This group, numbering between six and eight, but occasionally more, are the real source of the problem.
They are the oxygen that fuels the incitement of the few. They are the poor role models, the laughers of jokes, and the creators of tension.
The truth is, your difficult students don’t need any extra time or attention from you.
This idea that one or two students are creating most, or all, of the trouble and misbehavior in your classroom is a fallacy.
From the first day of school onward you must teach, model, and require exceptional behavior from all students. You must lock it down and button it up.
As your happy crew gets larger and larger, and the feeling of being part of something special grows stronger and stronger, no one will be able to resist its gravitational pull.
